..Southeast Arizona is having one of those picture-
perfect days with brilliant blue skies, spectacular mountain 
views, and temperatures that are not only refreshing, but 
inviting. It is the kind of morning that belongs on an old- 
fashioned postcard. Enjoy it, because the weather will turn 
considerably more active as two distinct systems bring stormy 
conditions back into Southeast Arizona late this week into the 
weekend.

The latest satellite imagery shows sunny skies across Southeast
Arizona, with GOES precipitable water imagery indicating a dry 
air mass with PWATs ranging from 0.25-0.45 inches. This dry air
mass has allowed for efficient radiational cooling, with 
minimum temperatures falling well into the 40s across many 
valley locations and into the lower to mid-50s around the Tucson
metro area.

The upper-air pattern early this afternoon is defined by a trough
across the Pacific Northwest, a strong closed low over the 
eastern Pacific near 33N/141W, and generally zonal flow 
extending downstream into the Desert Southwest. Not much has 
changed over the past several numerical model runs regarding the
evolution of this pattern. An upper ridge building into the 
Gulf of Alaska will try to phase the upper-low in the PAC NW 
with the EPAC low, resulting in an amplified mean trough. 

Strong northerly flow developing on the backside of this trough
will help weaken the closed circulation over the Eastern 
Pacific, eventually allowing this system shear out into the 
downstream zonal flow. Although this feature will weaken as it 
approaches, increasing southerly low to mid-level flow ahead of 
the trough will support a northward surge of tropical moisture 
through the Gulf of California into southwest Arizona Thursday 
night into Friday.

The 27/12Z deterministic GFS continues to indicate modest 850-700
mb moisture flux convergence from Tucson west and northwest 
between 30/18Z and 31/00Z Friday. This convergence, combined 
with decent deformation/ascent aloft ahead of the approaching 
weakening shortwave should support scattered showers and 
thunderstorms. Activity could begin as early as Thursday night, 
but the better opportunity will be during the day Friday as the 
moisture plume spreads north then northeast across Southeast 
Arizona.

Rainfall amounts with this first system will generally range from
a quarter to a half inch across much of the CWA. However, the 
orientation of the moisture plume within the prevailing 
southerly flow raises the potential for repeated rounds of 
showers and thunderstorms, especially across northern Pima 
county and SE Pinal resulting in locally heavier rainfall 
amounts. This solution matches the Weather Prediction Center Day
4 Excessive Rainfall Outlook (ERO) for Friday, which has these 
areas in a slight risk of exceeding flash flood guidance. 

Another shortwave will reinforce the mean trough over the Eastern
Pacific late Friday into Saturday, with another closed low 
developing Saturday afternoon before shifting east toward 
Arizona Sunday. This system will tap into a deeper plume of 
subtropical moisture as it approaches. The latest ECMWF ensemble
mean indicates a more pronounced moisture plume compared to 
previous runs, with PWAT anomalies reaching 3.5 to 4.5 standard 
deviations above normal. Given this anomalous moisture and the 
duration of the event, this is shaping up to be a significant 
precipitation event for Arizona. Strong southwesterly upslope 
flow will likely focus the heaviest precipitation across central
Arizona, especially along the Mogollon Rim Sunday. Across 
Southeast Arizona, increasing moisture and more widespread 
deformation/ascent aloft ahead of the trough axis will support 
widespread showers with embedded isolated/scattered 
thunderstorms. The northern portions of our CWA, including SE 
Pinal, Graham, and Greenlee counties remain favored for the more
substantial precipitation with this second event.

In general, periods of moderate rainfall with pockets of heavier
rain will produce storm-total amounts of three-quarters to one 
inch in the valleys and 1 to 2 inches in the mountains. Locally 
heavier amounts near 3 inches will be possible along southwest-
facing slopes of the higher terrain from Tucson north and 
northeast, including the Catalina and Rincon Mountains.

Although much of this rainfall will occur over a longer duration,
the cumulative runoff will likely result in flows through 
normally dry washes and water across roadway dips and other low-
water crossings. Significant ponding will also be possible in 
low-lying and poor-drainage areas. Embedded heavier rainfall 
could produce more rapid rainfall runoff and localized flash 
flooding. More substantial flows may develop in the creeks and 
rivers across northern Graham and Greenlee counties, including
